facts.claim: The English word bankrupt comes from Italian banca rotta, literally 'a broken bench', from banca, 'moneylender's shop', literally 'bench'; rotta is from Latin rupta, from rumpere, 'to break'.

corroboration.name: Merriam-Webster Dictionary, bankrupt (etymology: Old Italian bancarotta, from banca + rotta)

facts.claim: The word is said to come from an old custom of breaking the bench of bankrupts, but the allusion probably is figurative.

corroboration.name: The Gazette (official public record), the history of bankruptcy: 'the bench was broken in a symbolic show of failure'

facts.claim: In 1542, during the reign of Henry VIII, Parliament passed what scholars generally consider England's first bankruptcy law; debtors could be punished by imprisonment and, by 1705, death.

source.name: Constitution Annotated (Congressional Research Service), Historical Background on the Bankruptcy Clause

facts.claim: The Act of 4 & 5 Anne, passed in 1706, made fraudulent bankruptcy (hiding assets from creditors) a capital offense, and the same act introduced the discharge of debt.

source.name: Emily Kadens, The Last Bankrupt Hanged: Balancing Incentives in the Development of Bankruptcy Law, Duke Law Journal 59 (2010)

corroboration.name: Constitution Annotated (Congressional Research Service): debtors could be punished by, by 1705, death

facts.claim: In 1705-1706 Parliament made the bankrupt's refusal to cooperate with the commissioners running his bankruptcy a capital crime; almost as an afterthought, it also introduced discharge of debt. Coercing the debtor to be honest proved a failure; incentivizing cooperation with discharge would have a fruitful future.

source.name: Emily Kadens, The Last Bankrupt Hanged, Duke Law Journal 59 (2010), abstract

facts.claim: The London Gazette of 6 May 1760 gave notice that a commission of bankrupt had been awarded against John Perrott, of Ludgate Hill, London, Merchant.

source.name: The London Gazette, issue 9998, 6 May 1760, page 4

corroboration.name: The Newgate Calendar, John Perrott (a shop on Ludgate Hill from about 1752)

facts.claim: At Perrott's 1760 bankruptcy examination, the commissioners' interrogatory stated: there is a deficiency of the sum of 13,513 pounds.

source.name: Emily Kadens, Perrott Bankruptcy, Part 2, Credit Slips (2007)

corroboration.name: The Newgate Calendar, John Perrott: a deficiency of thirteen thousand, five hundred and thirteen pounds

facts.claim: The other halves of four banknotes were found tied up in a rag at the bottom of Perrott's trunk in Newgate prison, along with half of a 1,000-pound note.

source.name: Emily Kadens, Perrott Bankruptcy, Part 3, Credit Slips (2007)

facts.claim: John Perrott was hanged for fraudulent bankruptcy on Wednesday, November 11, 1761, at the ancient hanging place in West Smithfield, London.

source.name: Emily Kadens, The Last Bankrupt Hanged, Duke Law Journal 59 (2010)

corroboration.name: The Gazette: John Perrott was one of the few people in England hanged for fraudulent bankruptcy

facts.claim: Likely only four Englishmen were hanged for fraudulent bankruptcy between 1706 and 1820; the last was hanged in York in 1813, and the death penalty for the crime was abolished in 1820.

source.name: Emily Kadens, The Last Bankrupt Hanged, Duke Law Journal 59 (2010)

facts.claim: At Perrott's trial a witness, Harris, testified that she saw Ferne cut banknotes in half and give one half to Perrott; Ferne kept the matching halves, and searchers found halves of five notes at Ferne's.

source.name: Emily Kadens, Perrott Bankruptcy, Part 3, Credit Slips (2007)

facts.claim: £13,513 in 1760 has a real price (RPI) value of £2,870,000 in 2025 by MeasuringWorth's UK calculator; the ONS composite price index gives about £3,541,898 in 2026. Both are about 3 million pounds.

source.name: MeasuringWorth, Five Ways to Compute the Relative Value of a UK Pound Amount, 1270 to Present (real price, 1760 to 2025)

corroboration.name: officialdata.org, UK inflation calculator, 1760 (ONS composite price index)

facts.claim: In England and Wales today, a bankrupt is usually released ('discharged') automatically from bankruptcy restrictions and debts after 12 months.

source.name: GOV.UK, Becoming bankrupt: when bankruptcy ends
